query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: For FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy thin coatings, accelerating the cooling rate during deposition (relative to the baseline process) promotes the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline, twin‐rich near-surface layer that mediates a dynamic amorphization mechanism. This refined microstructure leads to reduced localized shear deformation and enhanced wear resistance under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating produced under standard deposition conditions resulting in a relatively coarser microstructure with lower twin and defect density.
generation.intervention: Increase the cooling rate during deposition (or via a subsequent rapid quench treatment) to promote an ultra‐fine grain structure with abundant twins and grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear regime (e.g., operating temperatures above 400–500°C) where dynamic microstructure evolution and thermal activation of deformation mechanisms are significant.
generation.structural_mediator: An ultra‐nanocrystalline, twin‐rich near-surface layer that forms as a result of rapid solidification and dynamic amorphization.
generation.mechanism: The refined microstructure increases grain boundary density and twin interfaces, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion. This leads to a mitigated inverse Hall-Petch behavior that reduces local shear localization and plastic deformation during sliding, thereby decreasing wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings processed with the increased cooling rate should exhibit lower wear volume (improved wear resistance) and reduced severity of microscopic deformation (fewer or smaller stress drops/deformation events) during high-temperature sliding tests compared to baseline coatings.
generation.baseline: Coating fabricated under standard cooling/deposition conditions resulting in a coarser microstructure with lower density of twins and grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The predictions are expected to hold during high-temperature sliding conditions typical of operating regimes (above ~400–500°C) where thermal activation contributes to microstructural evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the wear reduction and microstructural refinement may depend sensitively on the exact cooling rate and processing variables. Furthermore, the transition temperature at which the mechanism dominates over other high-temperature effects remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu thin coatings on a metal substrate: one produced via standard deposition conditions (baseline) and a second set processed with an increased cooling rate (intervention). Subject both sets to controlled high-temperature (e.g., 500°C) sliding wear tests under identical load and speed conditions. Perform detailed microstructural characterization (grain size, twin density analysis via TEM/SEM) before and after wear tests.
measurements: Wear volume or wear rate measured by profilometry or weight loss tests
Microstructural characterization (grain size distribution, twin density, defect analysis) using TEM/SEM
Friction coefficients recorded during sliding tests
Stress-strain behavior if accessible via nanoindentation or micro-scratch testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the intervention coatings (with increased cooling rate) do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and show no evidence of an increased twin or ultra-nanocrystalline structure compared to the baseline coatings under high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesized mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating showed a volume wear rate of (0.38 ± 0.08) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1, which is about half that of the AlCoCrFeNiTi coating in our previous study (0.77 ± 0.01) × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1 [] at the same test conditions. This result indicates that the wear resistance of the AlCoCrFeNiSi coating was better than that of the AlCoCrFeNiTi coating. Besides, comparing with the conventional flame-sprayed NiCrBSi coating with a volume wear rate of about 1.7 × 10−4 mm3·N−1·m−1 [], the coating in this paper also showed much better wear resistance. All of these results make the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi coating a promising one that can be used in abrasion environments in the industries of petroleum, power, mining, and so on. Besides the high density of the coating and the high hardness of the AlCoCrFeNiSi material, formation of the hard tribofilms (Figure 13) can be another reason for the good wear resistance.

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

High-velocity oxygen fuel spraying technology has higher particle velocity, lower flame temperature and fewer unmelted particles than atmospheric plasma spraying, which can prepare anticorrosive and wear-resistant coatings with low oxidation degree, good bonding rate and low porosity [,]. Cold spraying technology relative to the traditional thermal spraying technology, as well as the use of less thermal energy and more kinetic energy, greatly improves the impact speed of spraying particles on the substrate surface, and still keeps them in a solid state [,]. Nikbakht et al. selected equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy powders to study the particle-bonding mechanism during cold spray deposition []. The results show that the impact morphology of particles is related to strain rate, in addition to material and microstructure. Due to the dynamic inertial effect, severe plastic deformation occurred in the lower half of the particles, and deformed nanotwins with a thickness of about 200 nm were observed.
